newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire refugees reach Kisangani, say more on way.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugees reach Kisangani, say more on way.

text.p: Civilians fleeing a Tutsi revolt in east Zaire are starting to trickle into the town of Kisangani, hundreds of kilometres (miles) away, saying many more displaced Zaireans and Hutu refugees are on their way.

A spokeswoman for the U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) said in the capital Kinshasa that 60,000 displaced civilians were reported in the town of Lubutu on the road between Kisangani and the conflict zone.

But Roman Catholic Church workers and local businessmen who are trying to help the new arrivals in Kisangani say so far there is no concrete evidence here of a mass exodus across the forest wilderness leading from the east.
"A lot of people set off but the vehicles soon broke down or ran out of fuel and they had to come by foot," said Bujiriri Ruhagauka, a 33-year old customs clerk from Bukavu.
Ruhagauka left Bukavu, now under rebel control, in a truck with his wife and children and his brother's family. The party of 12 had to abandon the truck over 70 km (45 miles) from Kisangani.
Kisangani is the last outpost of tenuous Zairean authority before many thousands of square kikometres (miles) of forest and hills.
Thousands of displaced Zaireans and Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are believed to have left Bukavu and Goma, also in rebel hands, heading west into the forest and hills.

"Lots of people are at Walikale (over 300 km from Kisangani)," Ruhagauka said. "When they got there the refugees started to ask: Where do we go? What do we do? By now they must be between Walikale, Lubutu and Kisangani," he added.
Rwandan Hutus were among those fleeing east, he added.

In the capital Kinshasa, UNICEF spokeswoman Danielle Maillefer, told reporters 60,000 displaced people were in Lubutu. She quote church sources but said it was unclear whether they were displaced Zaireans or Hutu refugees.
UNICEF and the International Committee of the Red Cross plan to use Kisangani as a base to help the refugees and displaced.
With the scale of the problem still unclear, the Roman Catholic charity Caritas said at least 50 displaced Zaireans had arrived in this town of 500,000 people on Sunday night.
"We have to be able to treat their medical problems and feed them, and especially as more arrive we need to have them in one place," said Caritas administrator Claude Olenga.
Olenga was unable to give an exact number for those now in Kisangani. Informal estimates put the number at hundreds.
"When the needs become known and the security situation improves we will be able to respond with specialist help," ICRC spokesman Andreas Fuog told Reuters.
The charity Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors without Frontiers) has also sent an exploratory mission to Kisangani.
The main road from Goma and Bukavu to Kisangani was used as a line of retreat for troops from the battlefront.
Flights over the area revealed few people on the road, but also that the villages were deserted.
"As the soldiers pass through they look for food, so the villagers spend the day under the trees," said Kisangani Governor Lombeya Bosongo.

Kisangani was quiet on Monday after two nights of shooting and sporadic looting on Friday and Saturday. The local military commander warned troops from the warfront on Sunday that if they carried weapons on the street they would be shot.
